description: I think natural areas like things are kind of interesting as a thought experiment. At a glance, one can see that the vast majority of the biomass is comprised of natives, and a pretty diverse selection at that. In the overstory there is Oak (largely White and Red, some Bur), as well as Basswood, Hackberry, Bitternut Hickory, Black Cherry, Elm and some Paper Birch, Aspen, and Black Ash. The understory trees are also varied but is mostly Ironwood (Ostrya virginiana). In spring, the ground is littered with spring ephemerals which we are taught are sign of a healthy ecosystem. Sedges line the forest floor and while invasives (Garlic Mustard, buckthorn, etc.) are present, they are largely kept under reasonable control. I would guess this is due to be outshaded by native plants and perhaps the presence of a healthy mycorrhizal network. A healthy ecosystem, right? If you’re looking at simply the presence of natives vs. non-natives, sure. But all of the oaks are ancient and many knocking on deaths door. The recruitment of new oaks is non-existent, and has been so for 40+ years. While spring ephemerals are beautiful, how many of them are actually serving purpose to a large number of wildlife and insects? And what will happen when the large oaks inevitably disappear? Land managers are in a tough position, and I don’t blame them for their decision making. That is implying they even have a choice. Nevertheless, I think it’s important we ask ourselves if our traditional hand-off approach is best in a situation like this.
